prompt: Some people believe that governments should place a heavy tax on foods that are high in sugar and fat in order to improve public health. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
essay:
Several governments have introduced levies on sugary drinks, and there are recurring proposals to extend the principle to processed foods high in fat. I agree that taxation of this kind is justified, although its value lies less in the revenue it raises than in the change it forces further up the supply chain.

The first argument is that price is the most reliable lever a government has. Public information campaigns about diet have been running for decades with modest results, whereas a change at the till is felt immediately and by everyone. Tobacco duty demonstrates the mechanism: consumption tends to fall fastest among the young and the price-sensitive, which are precisely the groups whose long-term health is most at stake.

The second argument concerns reformulation. Where a levy is banded by sugar content rather than applied at a flat rate, manufacturers have a strong commercial reason to cut sugar in order to fall into a lower band, and a number of them have done exactly that. The health gain then reaches consumers who never altered their shopping at all, which is a far larger group than those who respond to price.

The standard objection is regressiveness: a flat levy takes a larger share of a small income than of a large one. This is true, and it is why the destination of the revenue matters. Directing the proceeds to school meals, sports facilities or subsidies on fresh produce returns the money to the households that paid most of it.

In my view, therefore, the tax is defensible provided it is designed to push reformulation and its revenue is directed back towards the communities most affected. A levy that simply raises the price of an unchanged product would deserve the criticism it attracts.
title: Taxing sugar and fat
